hook.text: Here's an easy question. How many words are in this sentence?

questions.text: Is can't one word, or two? Does the period after Doctor end the sentence? Is the dollar sign a word?

human.text: You read it in a second. A computer gets one flat string of sixty-two characters.

implied.text: Nothing in it says where a word starts, where a sentence ends, or what any of it means.

nlp.text: Natural language processing, NLP for short, closes that gap. It turns unstructured text into structure a program can compute with.

ambig-in.text: Part of what makes that hard is ambiguity.

ambiguity.text: Language is full of it, and we resolve it so easily that we rarely notice.

lexical.text: One word can mean two things. A bank is the side of a river, or a place for money. That's lexical ambiguity.

structural.text: One sentence can group two ways. I saw the man with the telescope. Did I use it, or was he holding it? That's structural ambiguity.

referential.text: And a word can point two ways. The trophy didn't fit in the case because it was too big. What was too big?

answer.text: You know it's the trophy. A computer has no idea. That's referential ambiguity.

mess-in.text: Real text is also messy in plainer ways.

contractions.text: Contractions hide words. Don't is do, and not.

period.text: One period ends a sentence, shortens Doctor, and marks a decimal point.

casing.text: Apple, the company, isn't apple, the fruit.

forms.text: Run, runs, running and ran are four spellings of one idea.

units.text: And New York is one place, written as two words.

reasons.text: Each of these is the reason a later step exists.

split-in.text: So why not just split on the spaces?

split.text: Here's the lesson's sentence. I can't believe it's not butter, Mister Jones!

pieces.text: Python's split cuts at every space, and gives eight pieces.

glued.text: But can't stays whole, hiding its not. And butter keeps its comma, so it would count as a different word from plain butter.

tokens.text: NLTK's word tokenizer gives twelve tokens instead: words and punctuation, each on its own.

fixed.text: It cuts can't in two, so the negation shows, peels off the punctuation, and keeps Mister with its period.

real.text: Breaking text into words is a real problem, not a one-liner.

do-in.text: So what does an NLP system actually do?

layers.text: It adds structure in layers. Characters become tokens.

layers-up.text: Tokens get normalized, tagged with their part of speech, and turned into counts and patterns.

understand.text: None of this understands the text. It counts, matches and transforms. A spam filter scores words without knowing what they mean.

rules.text: A step can follow rules that write down what people already know, like a list of stopwords, the little words to skip.

readable.text: Rules need no training data, and you can read exactly why they did what they did.

learning.text: Or it can be learned from labeled examples. That's powerful, but opaque.

course.text: This course sticks to rules and counts, where the intuition lives.

pipe-in.text: And rules like these run in a pipeline.

pipeline.text: A pipeline is a fixed sequence of steps, where each step's output is the next step's input.

tokenized.text: Tokenizing this sentence gives thirteen tokens, punctuation included.

cleaned.text: Cleaning drops the comma and the exclamation mark. Eleven left.

stopped.text: Removing stopwords drops five little words. Six left.

lemmatized.text: And lemmatizing turns cats into cat, and dogs into dog.

list.text: After tokenizing, each step is one Python list comprehension. The code is easy. Choosing the steps is the hard part.

cleaning.text: Those are the cleaning steps, and they're much the same in every project.

analysis.text: Analysis comes after: counting, tagging, building features. It depends on your goal, and so should the cleaning, because most of its steps are optional.

order-in.text: The order you run them in matters, too.

order.text: Here's the lesson's tiny test: the word the, written three ways, followed by end is near.

order-a.text: Lowercase first, then remove stopwords, and every the is gone. End, near.

order-b.text: Remove stopwords first, and all three slip through. The stopword list is all lowercase, and none of the three is.

silent.text: Nothing crashed. You just got a list that looks fine, and is wrong. Order bugs are silent.

next.text: Every one of these steps works on tokens. So the first step of the pipeline is deciding where one word ends.
